title: Coffin of Bakenmut
medium: Gessoed and painted sycamore fig wood
movement: Ancient Egyptian funerary art (Third Intermediate Period)

image.credit: Cleveland Museum of Art, Gift of the John Huntington Art and Polytechnic Trust (1914.561)
image.license: Public domain. Released under the Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access program

altText: A large painted wooden coffin from ancient Egypt, covered with painted decoration. The coffin is made of sycamore fig wood coated with gesso and then painted.

source.verifiedBy: Cleveland Museum of Art open-access API record (title, date, medium, culture, credit line, description, did_you_know, CC0 status, image URL); no creator named by the museum

context: A painted wooden coffin from Thebes, Egypt, made around 1000-900 BCE in the Third Intermediate Period and now in the Cleveland Museum of Art. The museum calls it one of the finest examples of painted wooden coffins made for the priests of Amen.

descriptions.k: This is a very old painted wooden case from Egypt. It was made a very long time ago. Look for the painted patterns and shapes all over it. Which painted part do you like best?
descriptions.g12: This painted wooden coffin was made in ancient Egypt, about 3,000 years ago. Artists covered it with painted designs. The museum says coffins like it were made for priests. Look for patterns and pictures. Which painted part would you point to first?
descriptions.g35: This coffin was made in Thebes, Egypt, around 1000 to 900 BCE. It is made of sycamore fig wood covered with gesso, a smooth white coating, and then painted. The museum says it is one of the finest painted coffins made for priests of Amen. Look at the painted designs. Why would artists spend so much care on one coffin?
descriptions.g68: The Coffin of Bakenmut was made in Thebes in the Third Intermediate Period, around 1000 to 900 BCE. Its sycamore fig wood was coated with gesso and painted. The museum calls it one of the finest painted wooden coffins made for priests of Amen, and says a smaller coffin was originally placed inside it. How might the painted decoration show the care given to a coffin?
descriptions.g910: The Coffin of Bakenmut, made in Thebes around 1000 to 900 BCE, is gessoed and painted sycamore fig wood. The museum describes it as among the finest painted wooden coffins made for priests of Amen and notes that a smaller coffin originally fit inside it. Funerary objects like this were made with great care. How do the materials and painted decoration reflect the purpose of the object?
descriptions.g1112: Made in Thebes during the Third Intermediate Period, Bakenmut's coffin is gessoed and painted sycamore fig, described by the museum as one of the finest painted wooden coffins made for priests of Amen. It was designed as the outer layer of a nested set. How does thinking of a coffin as a made, designed object, and not only as a relic, change how you read its painted surface?

k.daily: Look at the painted patterns. Which pattern would you like to trace with your finger?
k.emotion: How does this old painted case make you feel, and what do you see that makes you feel that way?
k.observation: Point to the colors you can see painted on the wood. Which one do you see most?
k.analysis: Look at the whole shape. What shapes do you see in the painted parts?
k.line: Find a line in the painting. Does it go up and down, side to side or around?
k.shape: Find a shape that repeats. How many times can you count it?
k.color: Which color in the painted designs do you like best, and where do you see it?
k.texture: The wood was covered with something smooth before it was painted. How do you think it would feel to touch?
k.space: Show with your hands how big you think the coffin is. Is it tall, long or wide?
k.light: Look for a bright spot and a darker spot on the coffin. Which part looks brightest?
k.meaning: Artists painted this by hand a very long time ago. What do you think they wanted to show?
k.culture: This was made in Egypt, a place far away. What do you think life was like there long ago?
k.technique: The artists used paint and wood. What do you think they used to put on the paint?
k.personal: If you could paint a pattern on a wooden box, what would you paint?
k.critical: What is one thing about this painted coffin that makes you want to ask a question?

g12.daily: Why do you think the artists took so much time to paint this coffin with so many designs?
g12.emotion: What feeling do you get from the painted decoration, and which parts make you feel that way?
g12.observation: List five painted details you can find on the coffin, such as patterns, pictures or bands of design.
g12.analysis: How did the artist arrange the painted designs so that your eye moves across the whole coffin?
g12.line: Which painted lines are straight, which are curved, and how do they decorate the coffin?
g12.shape: Which shapes repeat in the painted designs, and how does repeating them make the coffin feel organized?
g12.color: How do the painted colors work together on the wooden surface of the coffin?
g12.texture: The wood was coated with gesso before painting. Why might the artist want a smooth surface?
g12.space: How does the coffin's form show that it was made to hold something inside?
g12.light: Where does the painted surface look bright, and where does it look darker?
g12.meaning: What might the painted pictures and symbols have meant to the people who made this coffin?
g12.culture: The museum says coffins like this were made for priests of Amen. What might that tell you about the people who ordered them?
g12.technique: Why might the artists have chosen sycamore fig wood for this coffin?
g12.personal: What would you want to ask the artists who painted this coffin?
g12.critical: How would the coffin look different if it had been left as plain wood?

g35.daily: Which painted details on the coffin show the most careful work, and how can you tell?
g35.emotion: What mood does the painted decoration create, and which features of the coffin support your idea?
g35.observation: Choose one section of painted decoration and describe its patterns, colors and shapes in detail.
g35.analysis: How are the painted designs arranged on the coffin to create order and balance?
g35.line: How do the lines in the painted designs guide your eye along the length of the coffin?
g35.shape: How does the shape of the coffin work with the painted designs to form one unified object?
g35.color: How do the colors used in the painted decoration make some areas stand out from others?
g35.texture: The museum says the wood was gessoed. How does gesso help create the surface for painting?
g35.space: How does the coffin's form show that it was designed to fit inside another case or hold something within?
g35.light: How might the way light falls on the painted surface change what you see?
g35.meaning: What might the painted decoration tell us about what the ancient Egyptians believed about death and what comes after?
g35.culture: The museum says it is a fine example of coffins made for priests of Amen. What does that suggest about the role of priests in society?
g35.technique: What skills would artists need to build a wooden coffin, coat it with gesso and paint it with such detail?
g35.personal: Why do you think people today take care to preserve and study objects this old?
g35.critical: What questions would you ask an archaeologist or curator to better understand this coffin?

g68.daily: Which parts of the coffin's design draw you in first, and how does the painted decoration hold your attention?
g68.emotion: How does the painted decoration create a feeling of reverence or solemnity, and which details support that?
g68.observation: Compare two different painted areas of the coffin. How do their designs and details differ?
g68.analysis: How does the arrangement of painted designs and symbols organize the coffin's surface?
g68.line: How do the lines of the painted designs emphasize the long form of the coffin?
g68.shape: How does the coffin's form relate to the decoration on its surface?
g68.color: How might the choice and arrangement of colors give the decoration clarity and visual impact?
g68.texture: How would the gesso layer have changed the wood's surface, and how does that affect the painted details?
g68.space: The museum says a smaller coffin was originally placed inside this one. How does that nested design affect how you think about the object's form?
g68.light: How might lighting in a museum or in a tomb have changed how the painted decoration appeared?
g68.meaning: Egyptian funerary art often used symbols with specific meanings. How could you find out what the symbols on this coffin meant?
g68.culture: The museum says coffins like this were made for priests of Amen. How might the object reflect their place in society?
g68.technique: How do the materials, sycamore fig wood, gesso and paint, show planning and craftsmanship?
g68.personal: How do you think it feels to study objects made for beliefs and traditions of another culture, and how can we do so respectfully?
g68.critical: What can we learn from a coffin that we cannot learn from written records alone, and what limits might there be?

g910.daily: How does the coffin's decoration show that the object was made with ceremony and care in mind?
g910.emotion: How does the painted decoration establish a tone appropriate to its purpose, and which visual choices create it?
g910.observation: Examine the painted surface closely. What do the details reveal about the planning and skill of the artists?
g910.analysis: How does the organization of painted designs create hierarchy and order across the coffin?
g910.line: How do the painted lines and contours work with the coffin's overall form to unify the object?
g910.shape: How does the coffin's three-dimensional form shape the way the decoration is arranged and read?
g910.color: How might color have worked as both decoration and meaning in the painted surface of this coffin?
g910.texture: How does the combination of wood, gesso and paint create a surface suited to detailed painted imagery?
g910.space: How does the coffin's role as the outer part of a nested set affect the way its design was planned?
g910.light: How might the museum's lighting differ from the conditions in which a coffin like this was originally used, and how does that affect what we see?
g910.meaning: How might the painted imagery connect to religious beliefs about the afterlife, and what would you need to confirm an interpretation?
g910.culture: The museum says this coffin was made for priests of Amen at Thebes. How does the object reflect religious and social roles in this period?
g910.technique: How do the choices of sycamore fig wood, gesso and paint reflect the resources and workshop practices available at Thebes?
g910.personal: How should museums present funerary objects so that they respect the people and cultures that made them?
g910.critical: What are the limits of interpreting an ancient object without written explanation, and how can a viewer reason carefully with the evidence in the object?

g1112.daily: How does the coffin work simultaneously as a practical container, a religious object and a work of art?
g1112.emotion: How does the visual language of the painted surface construct an atmosphere of ritual seriousness?
g1112.observation: Study the relationships among painted areas. What does the density of decoration suggest about priorities in the workshop that made it?
g1112.analysis: How does the compositional organization of the decoration reflect conventions of Egyptian funerary art, and where might it depart from them?
g1112.line: How do the painted contours articulate the relationship between the coffin's surface and its sculptural form?
g1112.shape: How does the interplay of the coffin's volume and its painted imagery challenge distinctions between sculpture and painting?
g1112.color: How might color symbolism, if documented, add to an aesthetic reading of this coffin, and how would you test that claim?
g1112.texture: How does the gesso ground transform sycamore fig wood into a painting surface, and what does that reveal about the workshop's technical knowledge?
g1112.space: How does the design of a nested coffin set affect the way we should read the decoration on the outer layer?
g1112.light: How do the conditions of display in a museum alter the visual experience of an object made for a different setting?
g1112.meaning: How should interpreters distinguish between what the object shows, what scholars infer and what remains uncertain about its imagery?
g1112.culture: What does the museum's description of this coffin as an example of coffins made for priests of Amen suggest about the institutions that shaped Theban art around 1000 BCE?
g1112.technique: How do the choices of material and technique reveal the economic and religious investment represented in this coffin?
g1112.personal: What ethical questions arise when objects made for funerary use are displayed in museums, and how can education address them?
g1112.critical: What kinds of evidence would you need to move from describing this coffin's decoration to making a reasoned claim about its meaning?

teacherNote.context: A painted wooden coffin made in Thebes, Egypt, around 1000-900 BCE (Third Intermediate Period, Dynasties 21-22) and now in the Cleveland Museum of Art. The museum calls it one of the finest examples of painted wooden coffins made for the priests of Amen, made of gessoed and painted sycamore fig.
directions: Have students design a repeating border pattern for a wooden box, then explain what the pattern means to them.
Ask older students to research what Egyptian funerary art symbols meant and compare their findings with what they can see on this coffin.
Discuss how museums can display objects made for another culture's funeral customs respectfully, and why that matters.
